title: Write a spec record and check it
description:
1. An agent, or the owner, writes a Markdown file under `specs/` with its YAML header (`id`, `kind`, `title`, `parent`, kind fields and `links`) and its body. A component names its `file` and a test its `run_by`.
2. They run `lathe check`, which reports each problem with the record it belongs to.
3. They fix the record until the check has no errors, and the change is reviewed in git like code.

title: Split a product into domains and check their names
description:
1. An agent, or the owner, reads the record format's section on domains, or follows the modeling skill's first step, and lists the product's business capabilities with the questions it gives.
2. They write one domain record for each capability, and put the technologies each one uses as layers in its Design stage.
3. They run `lathe check`, which warns of any domain whose title or code names a technology, and rename it for its capability.

title: Adapt the meta-model for a product
description:
1. The owner decides a product needs a kind or relation Lathe does not have, or a default kind to sit somewhere new.
2. They add rows to the product's `metaExtensions` CSVs, or change Lathe's own `meta/` files, and review the diff.
3. The next check loads the merged meta-model, checks it for consistency, and rechecks every record against it; structural warnings show where records do not yet fit, each mistake reported once.
4. Use cases are grouped into capabilities, and use cases or whole domains follow patterns, as the meta-model allows; a kind may be made a full or a proof-only obligation. The engineering rules the code follows are written as standards, which components and tests meet.

title: Write a flow as steps and check it
description: How a flow is written step by step and checked. Its steps say what each part carries out.

title: Open a record's file from the desktop app
description:
1. In the desktop app, the author opens a record and chooses Reveal in Finder, Open in editor or Copy ID, from the record's menu or the File menu.
2. The shell finds the record's file from its ID alone and reveals it, opens it in the chosen editor, or copies the ID.
3. The author edits the file, and the page reloads with the change.

title: Group a domain's endpoints into APIs and write its integrations
description:
1. An agent, or the owner, lists the resources the domain's endpoints serve, writes one `api` record for each under the domain, and changes each endpoint's `parent` to its API, keeping its ID.
2. They move each rule every endpoint of an API shares into one interaction requirement under the API, and the shared request and response shapes into the API's Shapes table.
3. For each outside system the domain exchanges with, they write an `integration` with its `system` and one interaction requirement per exchange.
4. They run `lathe check`, which reports a record under a parent its kind does not allow.

title: Write a technical flow and check it
description:
1. An agent, or the owner, writes a `design_flow` in the layer that does most of the work, with `deepens` naming the flow.
2. They write one `design_step` per step under it, in order and on its path, with the component it `uses`, what it `satisfies`, and its transaction, locks and statements.
3. They run `lathe check`, which reports step orders that clash or skip as `step-order` errors, a technical flow that deepens nothing as a warning, and counts each step's `satisfies` as design.

title: Fix the workspace after an edit
description:
1. An agent edits records, then runs `lathe check` (the Claude Code plugin's hook runs it after every spec edit).
2. The check prints errors first: broken records, tests whose files do not back what they claim to prove, and IDs cited in prose that no longer exist. The agent fixes each and runs the check again until there are no errors.
3. When a rule Lathe does not know yet keeps coming up, the agent adds a check: one SQL file in `lathe/checks/`, run in name order with the others.
4. The agent hands the work back to the owner with the check's last lines, so they can see what is still to do.

title: Add a product's own check
description:
1. The owner decides a rule belongs to their product, not to Lathe, such as "every endpoint has at least one interaction requirement".
2. They name a checks folder in `lathe.config.json`, `"checks": "lathe-checks"`, and writes the rule there as `01-endpoint-without-interaction-requirement.sql`: one `SELECT` over the loaded tables returning `(severity, check, record, message)`.
3. They run `lathe check`. Lathe's checks run first, then the product's; each of its problems is reported under `endpoint-without-interaction-requirement`, with the others.
4. Had they named the file after one of Lathe's checks, or written SQL that fails, `lathe check` reports an error naming the file instead.
5. They fix what the new check finds, here by writing each endpoint's interaction requirements, and rerun `lathe check` until it is clean.

title: Review problems while an agent edits
description:
1. While an agent edits records, the owner keeps the product's Checks page (`/<product-id>/checks`) open: every problem of the product, errors first, grouped by check, and the workspace's below.
2. Each time a record file or the engine's rules change, the page reloads `GET /api/spec` and shows the problems as they are on disk now.
3. They open a problem's record page to see the record and its problems, and go back to the list.
4. When a check is unfamiliar, they follow its code to the check's page in the format reference: what it asks, how to fix it, and every problem it reports now. From the record's side bar, its Kind leads to what the format says about that kind.

title: Walk a domain in the graph and trace a requirement
description:
1. The reader opens a domain in the Graph view and sees it framed in the one map, its children grouped by kind, such as "Use cases (5)".
2. They click a group, then from node to node, to walk the model, the camera gliding to each while nothing in the map moves, with the breadcrumb trail showing the way back.
3. At a requirement or domain rule they switch on trace mode and see only its chain: what fulfills it, the components that satisfy it, the tests that prove it and their files.
4. They open any node's record page to read it in full.

title: Read a record as wiki, graph or model, from the keyboard
description:
1. The reader opens quick find from the keyboard, types part of an ID or title, and opens the record at its one address.
2. They open and close the Wiki, Graph and Model panes with their shortcuts; following a link in any pane moves them all, and the side bar shows the record's facts.
3. On a domain or an aggregate they open the Model view and read its ERD, then click a box to go to that aggregate or entity.
4. They keep the record open in a tab with Ctrl+K then Enter, open another in the preview tab, flip between them with Ctrl+Tab, each as they left it, and close one with Alt+Shift+W.
5. They fold the side navigation away, go back with the usual key, and open the shortcut sheet or the command palette when they need a key they do not know.
6. Throughout, Tab reaches every control and lets go of it, focus stays where they were after each move and comes back to the opener when a dialog or a sheet closes, and the announcer tells a screen reader what changed.

title: Read a flow step by step
description: How the reader reads a flow written as steps, on its page and in the graph. Its steps say what each part carries out.

title: Move between products as spaces
description: How the reader works in one product and moves to another.

title: Look something up in the side bar
description: How the Reader uses the side bar. In the Graph view it is already open on Details: they move the pointer over the boxes and read each record's facts and traceability in turn, then open one with Open. In the Wiki view they open the side bar from the page bar, switch to Outline and jump to the Traceability section, then switch to History, see the uncommitted change at the top, open an older commit's diff, and load more. Their choices come back with the tab after a reload, while the Wiki view of another tab stays closed.

title: Read a domain's APIs and its technical flows
description:
1. The reader opens a domain's Interaction design folder in the nav and sees its APIs and integrations beside its flows and views.
2. They open an API and read its endpoints, with their methods and routes, and the requirements every endpoint shares.
3. They open an integration and read each exchange with its outside system.
4. In Technical specification, they open a layer's technical flow and read its steps path by path, with the component each uses and what it satisfies.

title: Fix a record where it is read
description:
1. The Owner, on a record's page, chooses Edit; the form opens in place with the record's columns, parent, links and part rows.
2. They change a field and a link, and Save: one write goes to the server, the page reloads with the change, and the data file shows a one-line diff.
3. A change the store refuses keeps the form open with the reasons beside the inputs; they fix it and save again.
4. From the parent's page they Add a child, or Remove a record after reading what still references it.

title: Start using Lathe in a product
description:
1. The owner installs the Lathe package in the product's repo, runs `lathe init` with the product's name and prefix, and sets up the merge driver for the data files.
2. They add the first domain and records with `lathe add` (or an Agent through the plugin's MCP tools), run `lathe check`, and open `lathe serve` to browse and edit them.
3. A tool of their own loads the same workspace in code with `loadWorkspace(root)` and reads its records, problems and coverage.

title: Learn a shortcut from where it is used
description: How the reader learns a shortcut without opening the sheet.

title: Choose and make a theme
description: How the reader settles on a look. They press g then t, arrow through the themes watching the app change, and keep one with Enter (or Escape to keep what they had). They switch Light, Dark or System from the palette. When no built-in suits them, they open Appearance from the nav's footer, duplicate the closest theme, adjust its colors, fonts and density with the app changing around them and warnings where text gets hard to read, then export it to share.

title: Read Lathe on a phone
description: How the reader reads a domain on a phone between meetings. They tap the search button in the top bar, type a use case's ID and tap the result. The wiki fills the screen under the title; they read its requirements, then tap Graph in the page bar. They pinch out, tap a component to see its name, and tap Open. They pull up the side bar to check its coverage gaps, drag it to full height, then swipe it away. The link at the top takes them up to the domain; the Pages button brings back the use case they started from.

title: Work on a product in the desktop app
description:
1. The reader opens a product folder from File › Open Product Folder, Open Recent, the Dock or Finder, and it opens in a window of its own, on the shell color with a launch view until the specs answer.
2. The window draws Lathe's own title bar, with back and forward, the command center and the layout toggles, in the theme's colors.
3. They work from the native menus, whose choices run the app's commands by ID, and the Dock badge counts the errors of the product in front.
4. A folder the engine cannot load gets an error page with Retry, another folder and the folder itself.

title: Change Lathe and see the desktop app reload
description:
1. The owner runs `npm --prefix desktop run dev`, and each window loads the 5199 dev server when it serves the opened folder, or a dev server the shell starts for it.
2. A change to the app hot-reloads the page; a change to the main process or a preload restarts Electron.
3. A change to a record reloads the page in every mode.

title: Change the data through any writer
description:
1. An Agent calls the plugin's MCP tools, or the Owner runs `lathe add` or saves a form on a record's page, which sends `POST /api/write`.
2. Each writer hands the store's command layer one write; it checks the whole new state in one transaction, and refuses with every reason, or rewrites only the changed tables' files.
3. The server sees the data files change and sends `spec:changed`; open pages load the data again.
4. The change is reviewed and committed in git; a merge of two branches' data files goes through the merge driver row by row.

title: Read and close a domain's coverage gaps
description:
1. The owner runs `lathe check` and reads one coverage line per domain and obligation kind: designed, built, proved and planned.
2. Each gap names the obligation and what it lacks: a component that satisfies it, or a test that proves it. Pattern rules show once in each domain that follows their pattern.
3. An agent closes each gap with a component or a test in that domain, and the next check counts it.

title: See proof still owed and tests by state
description:
1. The owner runs `lathe check` on a product where some proved obligations still have planned tests.
2. Each obligation line where proof is still owed beyond what is unproved ends with how many have a planned test, such as `; 3/4 with a planned test`.
3. After each domain's obligation lines they read its tests by state, such as `LA-CHK tests: 99 automated, 0 manual, 0 planned`.
4. An agent reads the same counts from `lathe check --json`: `planned_any` on each obligation and `tests` on each domain's coverage.

title: Trace a requirement to the tests that prove it
description:
1. The reader picks a product in the Specs menu and sees its domain cards.
2. They open a domain, search for a requirement and open it.
3. On the record page they follow an incoming `proves` link to a test, and from the test its `run_by` file and its other `proves` links.
4. Below the body, its Traceability lists what designs, proves and carries it out, with a callout for each gap, linked to the check that reports it.

title: Read coverage for every obligation kind
description:
1. The reader opens a product and then a domain, and reads one coverage group per obligation kind: designed, built, proved and planned.
2. They open a gap, such as an interaction requirement at an endpoint that no test proves yet, on its record page.
3. On the record page each test that proves it shows its state: automated, manual or planned.

title: Check how a domain proves the patterns it follows
description:
1. The reader opens a domain page and unfolds **Patterns we follow**: each pattern the domain follows, with each of its rules marked designed, built and proved in this domain, or not applicable with the use case and reason.
2. They open a pattern from there: its page lists its settings, its rules and the domains and use cases that follow it, with each domain's proof status per rule.
3. Reading a rule's text, they follow a cited record ID in the prose to that record; an ID that no longer exists is shown as a broken link.
4. In the Graph view, the pattern's rules sit under the pattern and each following use case's `follows` link is drawn as a cross-link.

title: See proof still owed and tests by state
description:
1. The reader opens a product and reads each domain card's coverage: beside a planned bar, `1 more planned` says one obligation already proved still has a planned test; hovering explains it.
2. Under the bars they read the domain's tests by state, such as `Tests 12 automated, 1 manual, 2 planned`.
3. In the product's Summary they read the product's tests by state in total, and how many more are planned beside proof.
4. They open a domain and read the same on its Coverage section.
